newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Swedish, Russian baby talk helps babies talk.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Swedish, Russian baby talk helps babies talk.

text.p: The cooing, cheeping baby talk that adults the world over use on even the tiniest infants actually helps the young ones learn to talk, scientists reported on Thursday.

A study of so-called "parentese," the slow-spoken language with long, exaggerated vowel sounds that parents seem to naturally use on their babies, indicates it can help in the earliest analysis of words and aid in future pronunciation.
The study, published in this week's edition of the journal Science, tracked American, Swedish and Russian mothers as they spoke to infants and to adults.
Mothers from all three countries instinctively spoke parentese to babies, researchers found, and babies as young as 20 weeks old were apparently analysing their parent's speech.
"In normal, everyday speech adults generally race along at a very fast pace," Patricia Kuhl of the University of Washington in Seattle, one of the study's authors, said in a statement.

"But we know it is easier to understand a speaker when they stretch out sounds ... We also do this unconsciously with babies, giving them an improved verbal signal they can capitalise on by slowing down and over-articulating," Kuhl said.
In the study, the mothers from the United States, Sweden and Russia were all asked to speak to their infants, who ranged in age from two to five months, for 20 minutes.

Researchers told the mothers to include three vowel sounds common to all three languages: the "ee" sound as in "bead", the "ah" sound as in "pot" and the "uu" sound as in "boot". Russian, Swedish and English were chosen because they have substantially different vowel systems.

Parentese helps babies by letting mothers make vowel sounds distinct from one another, and gives a greater variety of vowel pronunciations without overlapping with other vowels, the researchers found.
This kind of speech helps babies learn their respective languages even though they cannot at first reproduce the sounds their mothers make.

"What infants are doing with this information is not memorisation," Kuhl said. "Their minds are not working like a tape recorder. Because their mouths and vocal tracts can't form the same sounds as adults, they have to transform adult sounds to frequencies they can use. So they must be analysing speech."
The good news is that the use of parentese is international and comes naturally, the researchers said.
